title: Dry-run: a Snowflake-style ID generator
intro: About 5 minutes. The whole generator is three shifts and two ORs — the interesting parts are the two failure modes you handle around it.

steps.title: Lay out the 64 bits before writing code
steps.explain: Draw the layout first and justify each field. The sign bit is deliberate — many languages have no unsigned 64-bit type, so a leading 1 would make the ID negative in Java and break every boundary it crosses.
steps.saysOutLoud: One sign bit, 41 of timestamp, 10 of machine, 12 of sequence.

steps.title: The generator itself
steps.explain: BigInt because the value exceeds 53 bits and would silently lose precision as a JS number — worth saying out loud, it is a real bug people hit. Note there is no network call anywhere in this function.

steps.title: Handle the clock moving backwards
steps.explain: This is the failure that turns a clever scheme into duplicate primary keys, and interviewers wait for it. NTP steps, VM resume, and manual fixes all rewind clocks. Advancing monotonically from the last issued timestamp keeps IDs unique; the embedded time is briefly ahead of reality, which nobody cares about.
steps.saysOutLoud: I never trust the wall clock directly — I advance monotonically from the last value I issued.

steps.title: Machine IDs come from the platform
steps.explain: The one piece of genuine coordination, and where deployments actually break. Two generators sharing a machine ID produce identical IDs whenever their clocks and sequences align. A ZooKeeper or etcd ephemeral lease claims the lowest free id and releases it if the process dies; a Kubernetes StatefulSet ordinal gives it to you free. Static config is fine at small scale and quietly dangerous at large, because someone will copy a config file.

steps.title: Decoding is free, and that cuts both ways
steps.explain: Because fields are positional, an ID is self-describing — given one from a bug report you know when and where it was made with no database lookup. The flip side is that it leaks creation time and generation rate, so use a separate opaque identifier for anything user-facing where enumeration matters.

steps.title: Be precise about the ordering guarantee
steps.explain: IDs sort by time within a machine and only approximately across machines — two generators in the same millisecond order by machine id, not by what actually happened first. That is fine for feeds and pagination, and saying where it is not fine is the mark of understanding rather than recall.

closing: If machine-ID assignment is impossible in your environment — some serverless platforms — offer UUIDv7 instead: time-ordered like Snowflake, zero coordination, at 128 bits rather than 64.
